paras: The lynching of Thomas Woodward took place about midnight on Saturday, August 16, 1890, when a mob took Woodward, a Black prisoner, from the jail at Humboldt, Tennessee, and hanged him. Woodward was accused of being one of three Black men who had assaulted and robbed a man named J. A. Greer two nights earlier. The killing was reported mainly through a brief wire dispatch, later picked up in columns of Afro-American news.

According to the Humboldt dispatch, J. A. Greer was assaulted and robbed on the Thursday night before the lynching by three men described as "negroes." Woodward was being held in the Humboldt jail on that accusation; one weekly digest described him as "charged with highway robbery." The coverage does not say what became of the other two men accused.

About midnight on Saturday a mob came to the jail, took Woodward out and hanged him. The Diamond Drill, a Michigan weekly, described the men as "a masked mob." The Detroit Plaindealer identified them as "a mob of white men" and said Woodward was "hanged to a tree." No report names any member of the mob, gives its size, or mentions the jailer or other officers.
No report of an inquest, arrests or official response appears in the coverage.

Most of the coverage was a single United Press dispatch datelined Humboldt, August 18, which ran almost word for word in daily papers in Washington, Maine, Michigan, Tennessee and North Carolina on August 18 and 19. Its headlines varied: "Taken From Jail and Lynched" in the Daily Critic and the Raleigh Daily State Chronicle, "Negro Lynched for Robbery" in the Evening Star, and "Negro Lynched" in the Clarksville Daily Tobacco Leaf-Chronicle. The Telegram-Herald headed it "A Tennessee Murderer Lynched," although the dispatch alleged only assault and robbery. The dispatch stated the robbery as fact and said nothing about the mob beyond its act.

The Clarksville paper, the only Tennessee paper found, printed the wire text without local detail. On August 23 the Diamond Drill condensed the story into one line of its "News of the Week," next to an item on the lynching of Henderson Fax near Trenton, Tennessee.

A differently worded version appeared on August 29 in the Plaindealer's "About Persons and Things," a column of news about Afro-Americans, and on September 6 in the Huntsville Gazette under "News and Sentiment (From Colored Exchanges)." These items were the only ones to give the mob's race, calling it "a mob of white men," yet they also stated flatly that "Woodward was guilty of assault and robbery" and added no comment. The Plaindealer printed the date as August 13, while the Huntsville reprint gave August 16, matching the wire.

The Humboldt dispatches placed the lynching about midnight on Saturday, August 16, while the Plaindealer gave August 13, a date before the Thursday-night robbery the wire described. Because the Huntsville Gazette's copy of the same item reads August 16, the earlier date is probably a printing error.

Every report says a mob took Woodward from jail and hanged him (A1, A7, A8); he was held on an accusation of assault and robbery, and no lawful authority or trial is reported (A2, A7).
The United Press wire dispatch (A1, A6) and a separately worded brief in an Afro-American news column (A8, reprinted as A9) agree on the core event, though the wire is a single underlying report.

framing.detail: Daily papers ran the short dispatch under headlines such as 'Negro Lynched for Robbery' and 'Taken From Jail and Lynched', treating the robbery charge as fact and making no comment on the mob.
The Telegram-Herald headed the same dispatch 'A Tennessee Murderer Lynched', though the text alleged only assault and robbery.
The Plaindealer and the Huntsville Gazette's 'From Colored Exchanges' column named the mob as 'white men' but also stated 'Woodward was guilty of assault and robbery', without comment.

versions.value: About midnight on Saturday (Aug. 16), per dispatches dated Aug. 18

conflicts.note: The wire dispatches, datelined Humboldt two days later, are the closer evidence; the Huntsville Gazette's reprint of the Plaindealer item gives August 16, so 'August 13' is probably a misprint, and in any case it falls before the Thursday-night robbery the wire describes.
